1. Which EVs have the highest range?¶

In [33]:
#Extracting Top 10 EVs by Range

top_range = df[['brand', 'model', 'range_km']].sort_values(
    by = 'range_km', 
    ascending = False
).head(10)

top_range
Out[33]:
brand model range_km
239 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ 685
194 Lucid Air Grand Touring 665
238 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450 4MATIC 655
241 Mercedes-Benz EQS 580 4MATIC 640
240 Mercedes-Benz EQS 500 4MATIC 640

In [38]:
plt.figure(figsize = (10,6))

sns.barplot(
    data = top_range,
    x = 'range_km',
    y = 'model',
    hue = 'brand',
    palette = 'Blues'
)

plt.title("Top 10 EVs by Driving Range")
plt.xlabel('Range (km)')
plt.ylabel('EV Model')
plt.legend(title = 'Brand')
plt.show()
Generating a horizontal bar chart using Seaborn to visually compare the top 10 electric vehicle models by their driving range in kilometers. The Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ ranks as the electric vehicle with the highest driving range in the dataset, reaching nearly 685 km. Mercedes-Benz models dominate the upper half of the ranking (holding multiple top spots like the EQS 450 4MATIC, EQS 580 4MATIC, and EQS 500 4MATIC), while Lucid (Air Grand Touring, Air Touring) and Audi (A6 Sportback and Avant series) also feature prominently among the top 10.

Lotus holds the top position with the highest average battery capacity, sitting just above 103 kWh. Luxury and performance manufacturers like Rolls-Royce and Cadillac follow closely behind, both averaging around 102 kWh.

3. Does a larger battery provide a longer range?¶

In [41]:
#Correlating battery capacity and driving range

df[['battery_capacity_kWh', 'range_km']].corr()
Out[41]:
battery_capacity_kWh range_km
battery_capacity_kWh 1.000000 0.880433
range_km 0.880433 1.000000

There is a strong positive relationship between battery capacity(kWh) and range(km) indicating that EVs with larger batteries tend to have greater driving ranges.

In [44]:
#Creating a scatter plot mapping battery capacity against driving range to examine how energy storage directly impacts vehicle distance capabilities.

plt.figure(figsize = (10,6))

sns.scatterplot(
    data = df,
    x = 'battery_capacity_kWh',
    y = 'range_km'    
)

plt.title('Battery Capacity Vs Driving Range')
plt.xlabel('Battery Capacity (kWh)')
plt.ylabel('Range (km)')
plt.show()
This diagram maps out individual EV models to display raw data points. It clearly illustrates a strong upward trend: as the battery capacity (kWh) increases, the overall driving range (km) increases proportionally.
In [67]:
plt.figure(figsize = (10,6))

sns.regplot(
    data = df,
    x = 'battery_capacity_kWh',
    y = 'range_km'    
)

plt.title('Battery Capacity Vs Driving Range')
plt.xlabel('Battery Capacity (kWh)')
plt.ylabel('Range (km)')
plt.show()
This diagram builds upon the scatter plot by overlaying a fitted linear regression trend line along with a shaded confidence interval band. It mathematically emphasizes the strong positive correlation between battery size and vehicle range, proving that larger battery capacity is the primary driver for extended driving distances in electric vehicles.

6. Does efficiency affect driving range?¶

In [57]:
#Investigating the relationship between vehicle energy consumption and overall driving range using correlation analysis or visualizing to determine how energy economy impacts distance capabilities.

df[['efficiency_wh_per_km','range_km']].corr()
Out[57]:
efficiency_wh_per_km range_km
efficiency_wh_per_km 1.000000 0.022943
range_km 0.022943 1.000000
The efficiency value of an EV does not show a strong direct linear relationship with its driving range in its dataset.
In [107]:
#Using jointplot with a hexagonal binning style to visualize both the individual distributions and the joint density/relationship between energy efficiency and driving range. 

plt.figure(figsize = (10,6))

sns.jointplot(
    data =df,
    x = 'efficiency_wh_per_km',
    y = 'range_km',
    kind = 'hex'
)

plt.xlabel('Efficiency (Wh/km)')
plt.ylabel('Driving Range (km)')
plt.show()

<Figure size 1000x600 with 0 Axes>
The vast majority of electric vehicles cluster heavily between 100-200 Wh/km in efficiency and 300-500 km in driving range, represented by the darkest blue hexagonal bins. But we cannot see any steep upward or downward linear trend between two variables.

plt.ylabel('Batter Capacity (kWh)')
plt.show()
In [66]:
#Plotting a regression plot featuring a fitted trend line and confidence interval to clearly display the positive linear relationship between charging power and battery size.

plt.figure(figsize = (10,6))

sns.regplot(
    data = df,
    x = 'fast_charging_power_kw_dc',
    y = 'battery_capacity_kWh'
)

plt.title('Fast-Charging Power Vs Battery Capacity')
plt.xlabel('Fast-Charging Power (kW)')
plt.ylabel('Batter Capacity (kWh)')
plt.show()
The correlation matrix shows a value of 0.728557, which indicates a strong positive linear relationship between fast-charging power and battery capacity.As seen in the regression plot, electric vehicles with larger battery capacities (higher kWh) tend to support significantly higher fast-charging power (higher kW DC). Conversely, cars with smaller batteries generally have lower fast-charging capabilities.

Front-Wheel Drive (FWD) vehicles record the highest average acceleration times, taking nearly 9.7 seconds on average to hit 100 km/h, typically reflecting more budget-friendly, city-oriented, or lower-horsepower EV configurations.

13. Which Charging ports are Most Common?¶

In [112]:
#Counting the frequency of different fast-charging port types and generating a Matplotlib pie chart to show the proportional distribution across the dataset.


port_counts = df['fast_charge_port'].value_counts()

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))

plt.pie(
    port_counts,
    labels=port_counts.index,
    autopct='%1.1f%%',
    startangle=90,
)

plt.title('EV Fast-Charging Port Distribution')
plt.show()
The pie chart clearly shows that the CCS (Combined Charging System) port is overwhelmingly the industry standard, accounting for 99.8% of the electric vehicles in the dataset. While CHAdeMO ports make up an extremely small fraction (0.2%), reflecting its phasing out in modern EV designs.
